subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 61-year-old woman has a chronic shallow ulcer with an irregular border and serous exudate over her medial malleolus. The surrounding skin shows varicose veins, edema, and brownish eczematous patches. She reports only mild discomfort.
question: Which of the following is the most likely ulcer type?
explanation_correct: Venous ulcers are the most common ulcer type and result from chronic venous insufficiency. They occur in the gaiter area (ankle to midcalf), typically over the malleoli, and are shallow with irregular borders and exudate. Pain is mild to moderate. Associated signs include telangiectasias, varicose veins, edema, and stasis dermatitis with erythematous eczematous patches.

explanation_incorrect.A: Arterial ulcers are painful, symmetric, punched-out lesions on distal toes or pressure points with absent pulses and cold pale skin.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neuropathic ulcers are painless, hyperkeratotic lesions over bony prominences in patients with peripheral neuropathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Pressure injuries occur over weight-bearing points such as the sacrum in immobile patients and range from non-blanchable erythema to full-thickness loss.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vasculitic ulcers are not one of the four classic cutaneous ulcer types and would not show the venous stasis changes described.

educationalObjective: A shallow exudative ulcer in the gaiter area with varices and stasis dermatitis is a venous ulcer, the most common type.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Cutaneous ulcers

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 72-year-old man has a small, symmetric, well-circumscribed 'punched-out' ulcer on his anterior shin that is extremely painful. Pedal pulses are absent, and the surrounding skin is cold, pale, and atrophic with loss of hair.
question: Which of the following is the most likely ulcer type?

options.text: Arterial ulcer due to peripheral artery disease

explanation_correct: Arterial ulcers result from peripheral artery disease, such as atherosclerotic stenosis. They occur on the distal toes, anterior shin, and pressure points and have a symmetric, well-defined punched-out appearance. Pain is severe, and associated signs of arterial insufficiency include cold, pale, atrophic skin, hair loss, and absent pulses. This contrasts with the relatively painless venous and neuropathic ulcers.

explanation_incorrect.B: Venous ulcers are shallow and exudative in the gaiter area with mild pain and stasis changes, not severe pain and absent pulses.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neuropathic ulcers are painless with hyperkeratotic undermined borders over bony prominences, unlike this very painful punched-out lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pressure injuries arise over weight-bearing points such as the sacrum in immobile patients, not on the anterior shin with absent pulses.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pyoderma gangrenosum is an inflammatory ulcer associated with systemic disease, not the classic ischemic picture described.

educationalObjective: A severely painful punched-out ulcer with cold pale hairless skin and absent pulses is an arterial ulcer from peripheral artery disease.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 57-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus has a painless deep ulcer over a metatarsal head with a hyperkeratotic edge and undermined borders. He has claw toes, Charcot joints, and absent ankle reflexes. Pedal pulses are palpable.
question: Which of the following is the most likely ulcer type?
explanation_correct: Neuropathic ulcers arise from peripheral neuropathy, most notably in the diabetic foot. They develop over bony prominences such as metatarsal heads and the heel, with a hyperkeratotic edge and undermined borders. Pain is absent because of sensory loss, and associated signs include claw toes, Charcot joints, and absent reflexes. Palpable pulses help distinguish this from an arterial ulcer.

explanation_incorrect.A: Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter area with mild pain and stasis changes, not over metatarsal heads with absent sensation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Arterial ulcers are severely painful with absent pulses and cold pale skin, whereas this patient has palpable pulses and no pain.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pressure injuries occur over weight-bearing points (sacrum, ischium, calcaneus) in immobile patients and are painful, unlike this painless foot ulcer.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vasculitic ulcers are not a classic category here and would not present with the neuropathic signs described.

educationalObjective: A painless hyperkeratotic ulcer over a bony prominence with absent reflexes and Charcot changes in a diabetic patient is a neuropathic ulcer.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 78-year-old woman who is bedbound after a stroke develops a non-blanchable erythematous area over her sacrum that progresses to full-thickness skin loss over several days. She develops fever and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and imaging suggests involvement of the underlying bone.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this lesion and its likely complication?

options.text: Venous ulcer over the gaiter area, associated with varicose veins
Arterial ulcer over a distal toe, associated with absent pulses
Neuropathic ulcer over a metatarsal head, associated with absent reflexes
Venous ulcer complicated by stasis dermatitis
Pressure injury over a weight-bearing point, with soft tissue infection and osteomyelitis as frequent complications

explanation_correct: Pressure injuries result from prolonged unrelieved pressure, typically over weight-bearing points such as the sacrum, ischium, and calcaneus in immobile patients. They range from non-blanchable erythema to full-thickness skin loss, and pain is present. Soft tissue infection and osteomyelitis are frequent complications, explaining this patient's fever and imaging findings. The other ulcer types are defined by vascular or neuropathic mechanisms rather than pressure.

explanation_incorrect.A: Venous ulcers occur in the gaiter area with shallow exudate and stasis changes, not over the sacrum of a bedbound patient.
explanation_incorrect.B: Arterial ulcers are painful punched-out lesions with absent pulses, not pressure-induced sacral breakdown.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neuropathic ulcers are painless hyperkeratotic lesions over foot bony prominences in neuropathy, not a sacral lesion in an immobile patient.
explanation_incorrect.D: Stasis dermatitis accompanies venous ulcers in the gaiter area, not a sacral pressure injury with suspected bone infection.

educationalObjective: Pressure injuries arise over weight-bearing points in immobile patients, present with non-blanchable erythema progressing to full-thickness loss, and frequently complicate with osteomyelitis.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Cutaneous ulcers

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 64-year-old man with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has a painless, deep ulcer on his heel with undermined borders and surrounding hyperkeratosis. Pedal pulses are normal, and there are no varices or stasis changes.
question: Which of the following findings most strongly supports a neuropathic rather than an arterial or venous cause?

options.text: Punched-out appearance with absent pedal pulses
Hyperkeratotic undermined borders over a bony prominence with absent sensation
Shallow exudative ulcer in the gaiter area with varices
Non-blanchable erythema over the sacrum in an immobile patient
Cold, pale, atrophic skin with hair loss and severe pain

explanation_correct: Neuropathic ulcers occur over bony prominences such as metatarsal heads and the heel in patients with peripheral neuropathy. They have hyperkeratotic edges with undermined borders and are painless because of sensory loss; claw toes, Charcot joints, and absent reflexes are associated. Normal pulses and the absence of stasis changes argue against arterial and venous etiologies. This patient's findings are classic for a diabetic neuropathic ulcer.

explanation_incorrect.A: A punched-out ulcer with absent pulses indicates an arterial ulcer, not a neuropathic one.
explanation_incorrect.C: A shallow exudative gaiter-area ulcer with varices indicates a venous ulcer.
explanation_incorrect.D: Non-blanchable sacral erythema in an immobile patient indicates a pressure injury.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cold pale atrophic skin with hair loss and severe pain indicates arterial insufficiency.

educationalObjective: Absent sensation with a hyperkeratotic undermined ulcer over a bony prominence identifies a neuropathic ulcer, especially with normal pulses.
